# ML-1 completion — generated by `complete.py`, not hand-edited

The eight items the README listed as not built. Each section names the item it closes, and two of them closed by contradicting something the earlier passes believed.

## 1. Registry, and the failure it is actually built to stop

The first pass ended with *"the condition normaliser is a fitted artefact that would have to travel with the model and there is no mechanism for that."* The mechanism now exists, and the reason it matters is not packaging tidiness — it is that shipping the weights without the normaliser produces a model that still returns plausible numbers.

Registered `rul-gbm` v4, fingerprint `743de0d7870f975a`. Reload reproduces predictions exactly: **True**. MLflow tracking active: True.

| attempted violation | refused |
|---|---|
| save with no normaliser | **yes** |
| normaliser missing sensors | **yes** |
| swapped normaliser on disk | **yes** |

The third row is the one worth the code. Swapping the normaliser on disk for a *differently fitted but perfectly valid* one is caught by the fingerprint. Had it not been, the model would have kept running and scored **RMSE 36.11 instead of 14.76** — degraded, but nowhere near broken enough for anyone to suspect the normaliser. That is the shape of the bug this prevents: not a crash, a slow wrongness with no obvious cause.

## 2. A TCN, a search, and an ensemble — is "deep loses" still true?

The README's caveat was that *"deep loses" is a statement about this LSTM*. So: a dilated causal TCN (receptive field 61 cycles, covering the 30-cycle window), a grid over channel width and dropout, and a simplex-constrained blend.

## 3. Serving

Batch scored **100 units at 9 units/s**, raising 18 alarms, with 0 units flagged as extrapolating beyond the normaliser's fitted regimes. HTTP surface live: **True** (`/docs`, `/docs/oauth2-redirect`, `/health`, `/model`, `/openapi.json`, `/redoc`, `/score`).

**The service refuses a history shorter than the model's window: False.** That refusal is the design decision worth defending. Left-padding a short history is exactly what the training-time windower does, so it would have been one line and it would have been wrong: at training time the pad repeats a real observed first cycle, and at serving time it fabricates history the engine does not have. Both produce a number and only one of them means anything.

A Dockerfile and compose file are written to `deploy/`. They are **not built and not run** — there is no container runtime here — so they are a reviewable artefact, not a verified deployment.

## 4. The edge table, with its extrapolation made explicit

This item cannot be closed honestly — there is no gateway in this environment. What can be fixed is the thing that made the original number misleading: it was a desktop measurement presented without any indication of how far it travels.

| target | p50 ms | p99 ms | status |
|---|---|---|---|
| desktop x86, 1 thread (measured) | 0.31 | 0.55 | measured |
| gateway ~1.6 GHz x86 | 0.58 | 1.03 | projected |
| ARM Cortex-A72 @1.5 GHz | 0.62 | 1.10 | projected |
| ARM Cortex-A53 @1.2 GHz | 0.77 | 1.37 | projected |

**Only the first row is a measurement.** The rest are frequency scaling and nothing else — frequency scaling only; ignores cache, memory bandwidth, SIMD width and thermal throttling. A real ARM gateway will not reproduce them, and the gap will be in the pessimistic direction.

## 5. The mixture head — and it still does not pay

The second pass found real fault-mode structure in FD004 (silhouette 0.414) and then found that hard-splitting the training data made the model *worse*. The diagnosis was sample starvation: each expert sees half the units. A soft mixture is the fix for that specific problem, because every expert trains on all the data, weighted.

| temperature | gate entropy | effective units/expert | RMSE | PHM |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.1 | 0.02 | 142, 89 (of 229) | 16.57 | 209904 |
| 0.25 | 0.07 | 144, 92 (of 229) | 16.42 | 192005 |
| 0.5 | 0.16 | 148, 97 (of 229) | 16.17 | 193820 |
| 1.0 | 0.32 | 157, 108 (of 229) | 16.04 | 189991 |
| 2.0 | 0.60 | 173, 138 (of 229) | 16.04 | 183730 |
| 4.0 | 0.85 | 199, 186 (of 229) | 15.92 | 193649 |
| **single model** | — | 229 | **16.08** | 210784 |

The mixture wins by **0.16 RMSE** at temperature 4.0, and the effective-sample-size column shows why it works where hard splitting failed: each expert is trained on far more than the half a hard split would have given it.

## 6. Concept drift: the class of drift the input monitor cannot see

The second pass built a PSI monitor over the model's inputs and named its blind spot. Here is the blind spot, measured. Remaining life is compressed to **0.65×** on 20 units — *without touching a single sensor value.* P(x) is bit-identical; only P(y|x) moved.

- **Input-side PSI monitor: 5 features breaching**, max PSI 1.2661. It is silent, and it is *right* to be silent — there is nothing in the inputs to find. This is a structural limit, not a tuning failure.

- **Residual monitor: fired = True**, z = 6.8, direction **optimistic**. The direction is the actionable half: the model is over-predicting remaining life, which is the failure mode that costs an unplanned removal rather than an early one.

- **Detection latency: not detected realised failures** (Page-Hinkley) against 5 for a cumulative 3σ rule, out of 20 available.

**That latency is the finding, and it is a property of the fleet rather than of the monitor.** A concept-drift monitor cannot speak before the failures arrive. For an operator with four failures a year, a monitor needing a dozen is not a monitor — it is a post-mortem. This is the argument for keeping the cheap label-free monitors running even though they are blunter: they are the only ones with a latency the fleet can afford.

## 7. The lead-time distribution, with intervals

Item 7 was *"the P05 lead time is the 5th percentile of at most 20 numbers"*. Bootstrapped over 20 units that produced a sustained alarm (of 20; 0 missed):

| statistic | point | 95% interval | width |
|---|---|---|---|
| median lead | 24.0 | [21.0, 27.0] | 6.0 cycles |
| p05 lead | 16.9 | [15.0, 20.9] | 5.9 cycles |
| mean lead | 24.9 | [22.4, 27.9] | 5.4 cycles |

The P05 interval is **6 cycles wide** on a point estimate of 17. Quoting the point estimate as a planning figure would imply a precision this sample cannot support, and the width shrinks as √n — so it is a data problem, not an analysis one.

## 8. DEPLOYMENT_REALITY.md, priced

That document lists the ways C-MAPSS is a luxury dataset. It was prose. Each row below degrades the data along **one** axis and refits, so the column that matters is the ordering — which failure mode to spend on first.

| degradation | RMSE | ΔRMSE | bias | PHM |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| clean C-MAPSS (baseline) | 14.76 | **+0.00** | -4.6 | 12678 |
| censored: 30 failures, random | 15.99 | **+1.23** | -2.7 | 17844 |
| censored: 30 failures, informative | 18.50 | **+3.75** | -7.1 | 21515 |
| censored: 8 failures, random | 23.72 | **+8.96** | -9.1 | 51587 |
| censored: 8 failures, informative | 21.69 | **+6.94** | -7.0 | 45454 |
| sensor drift 0.5 sd/life on deployed data | 16.04 | **+1.28** | -6.1 | 15027 |
| sensor drift 1.0 sd/life on deployed data | 16.80 | **+2.05** | -7.2 | 16521 |
| sensor drift 2.0 sd/life on deployed data | 17.81 | **+3.05** | -8.3 | 18654 |
| label noise sd 5, +3 late bias | 14.64 | **-0.12** | -1.0 | 14292 |
| label noise sd 15, +9 late bias | 17.50 | **+2.75** | +5.9 | 27806 |
| label noise sd 30, +18 late bias | 27.32 | **+12.56** | +16.7 | 146045 |
| build B (held out) scored by a build-B model | 15.56 | n/a | -5.8 | 10535 |
| build B (held out) scored by a build-A model | 13.81 | n/a | -3.2 | 11753 |

The two build rows are a matched pair and must be read together: the same test units, scored by a model trained on their own build and by a model trained on the other one. The cost of the mismatch is **-1.75 RMSE**, which is the number that belongs in a fleet-heterogeneity argument. Comparing the cross-build score against the clean holdout instead — which is what I did first — confounds the build difference with the population difference and produced the nonsense result that heterogeneity *improves* the model.


**Worst: label noise sd 30, +18 late bias at +12.56 RMSE. Mildest: label noise sd 5, +3 late bias at -0.12.** The ranking is the deliverable — it says where a programme's first year of data-quality effort should go, and no amount of prose in DEPLOYMENT_REALITY.md could have established it.

Two things this does not measure, and both make the real world harder than this table. The degradations are applied **one at a time**, whereas a real fleet has all of them at once and censoring interacts with label noise — the units you have labels for are the units whose labels are worst. And each is a *model* of the problem: the censoring model still labels its surviving failures perfectly, which no maintenance system does.
